strengths: The paper targets an important and under-addressed failure mode in gloss-free sign language translation: fingerspelled names/technical terms and asynchronous non-manual facial cues. This is a meaningful computer vision and accessibility problem.

The proposed modular design, with separate continuous-sign, fingerspelling, and lip-reading streams followed by temporal fusion and LLM decoding, is intuitively well motivated and could be a useful direction if validated rigorously.

The manuscript attempts a broad evaluation across How2Sign and ChicagoFSWildPlus, includes component ablations for lipreading, LLM decoding, glossing choices, and temporal alignment, and provides qualitative examples that illustrate the intended behavior of the system.
The reported numbers, if produced under a fair protocol, would be substantial improvements, especially the BLEU-4 gain on How2Sign and the letter accuracy gain on ChicagoFSWildPlus.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is not convincing enough to support the strong state-of-the-art claims. Critical protocol details are missing: exact train/validation/test splits, preprocessing choices, sequence-type labels, pseudo-gloss construction, LLM fine-tuning data, decoding settings, compute, hyperparameters, and whether any evaluation data or transcripts are seen during staged training.

Comparisons appear potentially unfair or under-specified. The method uses multiple pretrained/fine-tuned components, lipreading, fingerspelling supervision, pseudo-glossing, and an LLM, but the baseline table does not clearly normalize for modalities, external data, model scale, or training data. This makes the large reported gains difficult to interpret.

The method description has substantial technical ambiguities and inconsistencies. It is unclear whether routing is per-sequence or per-token, how CTC outputs become aligned embeddings for fusion, how differing temporal resolutions are reconciled, how the fusion CTC target differs from the final translation target, and how the LLM consumes continuous fused representations versus discrete tokens.

Several details raise reliability concerns: Figure 1/caption appears to describe mainly the lipreading subsystem rather than the full method; citations are sometimes inappropriate or confused; the How2Sign size is stated as over 8080 hours while the described components sum to roughly 82 hours; and there are repeated typographical and factual inconsistencies.

The ablations are too limited for the claims. There is no comparison to simpler late fusion, no oracle sequence-router analysis, no error breakdown specifically for names/fingerspelling in full SLT, no robustness analysis across signers, and no evidence that improvements come from visual grounding rather than LLM language priors.

The use of lipreading in fingerspelling evaluation is not clearly justified for ChicagoFSWildPlus, and the paper does not explain whether mouth regions are visible, annotated, or temporally aligned in that dataset. This weakens the central claim that lip cues disambiguate fingerspelled letters.

Reproducibility is poor. The paper lacks architecture sizes, optimizer schedules, batch sizes, frame sampling, token vocabularies, CTC decoding details, LLM adaptation method, release plan, and enough implementation detail to replicate the results.

The writing and presentation need significant polishing. Many grammar issues, duplicated references, malformed statements, and imprecise definitions make it harder to assess technical soundness. These are not merely cosmetic because they obscure the actual training and evaluation pipeline.

strengths: The paper targets an important and under-addressed problem in sign language translation: proper handling of fingerspelling and non-manual cues such as mouthing/lip movements, which are genuinely important for names, technical terms, and disambiguation.

The high-level modular idea of separate continuous-sign, fingerspelling, and lip-reading experts followed by fusion and LLM decoding is reasonable and, if rigorously implemented and evaluated, could be a useful direction for gloss-free SLT.

The manuscript includes comparisons to recent SLT and fingerspelling work, component ablations, temporal-shift ablations, and qualitative examples, which are the right kinds of evidence to attempt for this contribution type.
weaknesses: The evidence is not convincing enough to support the central claims. The reported gains are very large, e.g. BLEU-4 23.5 on How2Sign versus 15.5/14.9 for strong baselines, but the paper gives insufficient training, split, preprocessing, decoding, hyperparameter, checkpoint, and evaluation details to establish comparability or reproducibility.

The experimental protocol is internally unclear and possibly flawed. The paper says it pre-trains on YouTube-ASL and ChicagoFSWild+ and fine-tunes on How2Sign, but also claims evaluation on YouTube-ASL without showing such results. The construction of sequence-type labels, fingerspelling labels, pseudo-gloss labels, and lip/phoneme targets for full SLT videos is not adequately specified.

There is a serious risk of label leakage or unrealistic supervision in the pseudo-glossing and LLM stages. The method removes “unneeded” text from labels and lets an LLM select important words, then fine-tunes another LLM to reconstruct sentences from fusion outputs. It is not clear what information is available at inference time, how pseudo-glosses are derived without using target translations, or whether the BLEU gains reflect visual understanding rather than language-prior reconstruction.

The model description is inconsistent and under-specified. Figure 1 appears to describe only a lipreading phoneme pipeline, while the text claims a three-stream sign/fingerspelling/lip architecture. The fusion equations mix token logits/embeddings with different temporal lengths without explaining alignment, padding, CTC decoding, or how gradients and frozen modules interact. The claimed hard Gumbel routing is also not clearly trained or supervised.

The ablations are too shallow to validate the proposed mechanism. Only “without lipreading,” “without LLM,” LLM size, glossing method, and synthetic temporal shifts are reported. There are no controls for DINOv2 backbone strength, LLM-only/text-only reconstruction, sign-only versus fingerspelling-only routing, oracle routing, pose/RGB differences, or equivalent-capacity single-stream baselines.

The sequence classification accuracy of 99.2% is reported without a table, dataset definition, class distribution, temporal granularity, or confusion matrix. Since “rest” and continuous signing may dominate, this number is not interpretable and may not support the claimed routing quality.

The fingerspelling comparison on ChicagoFSWildPlus is not sufficiently grounded. The paper reports 73.2% letter accuracy, but does not specify the train/test split, signer independence, preprocessing, lexicon constraints, beam search/language model use, or whether the lipreading stream is available and fair relative to prior hand-centric baselines.

Several dataset and citation details reduce confidence. How2Sign is described as “8080 hours” while also listing 79.1h and 2.96h subsets; there are duplicate or odd references, questionable citations for ViT-base and LLMs, repeated CTC references, and many writing errors. These do not by themselves decide the paper, but together with the technical gaps they undermine trust in the implementation and evaluation.

The paper lacks meaningful discussion of limitations, failure modes, Deaf-community considerations, privacy, consent, deployment risks, and language coverage. Given the application domain and the use of face/lip data from signers, this omission is important.

Overall, although the motivation is strong, the manuscript does not provide a technically sound, reproducible, or sufficiently credible scientific case for the claimed state-of-the-art performance. I would recommend rejection.

strengths: The paper targets an important and under-addressed weakness of gloss-free sign language translation: poor handling of fingerspelling and non-manual facial/lip cues. The motivation is compelling and well aligned with real ASL use cases such as names, technical terms, and disambiguation.

The proposed modular multi-stream design is sensible: separating continuous signing, fingerspelling, and lipreading before fusion is a plausible way to reduce the burden on a monolithic video-to-text model. The learned fusion/alignment component is particularly relevant for asynchronous manual and non-manual signals.

The reported empirical gains are strong. The method substantially improves over prior How2Sign results in BLEU-4 and ROUGE, and also improves letter accuracy on ChicagoFSWildPlus. The ablations support the main claims that lipreading, the LLM decoder, pseudo-glossing, and learned temporal alignment each contribute materially.
The supplementary qualitative examples are useful and make the intended behavior of the system concrete, especially for proper-name recovery through fingerspelling plus lipreading.
The paper is mostly easy to follow at the high level and addresses a socially meaningful accessibility problem with clear potential impact if the approach proves robust.
weaknesses: Reproducibility and implementation detail are not yet sufficient for a convincing systems/algorithmic paper. Critical details are missing or underspecified, including exact train/validation/test splits, preprocessing heuristics, sequence-type labels, hyperparameters, LLM fine-tuning protocol, prompt/prefix design, decoding settings, and whether all baselines use comparable data and supervision.

The comparison may not be fully fair. The proposed method uses specialized fingerspelling/lipreading supervision, pseudo-glossing, and a large LLM, while several baselines may not have access to the same auxiliary signals or pretraining. The paper should more explicitly separate gains from architecture, extra supervision, pretraining scale, and LLM capacity.

Some technical descriptions are internally unclear. The equations mix CTC logits, token embeddings, and fused representations without always specifying dimensions or how variable-length CTC outputs are aligned. The sequence classifier appears described as clip-level in one place but token/time-varying in the fusion and visualizations. The final LLM interface from fusion outputs to text is also vague.

The ablations are helpful but incomplete. There is no comparison against simpler late-fusion or concatenation baselines, no end-to-end vs staged-training comparison, no analysis by fingerspelled/non-fingerspelled segments, no signer/generalization breakdown, and no statistical significance or confidence intervals for the large reported gains.

The manuscript contains several presentation and factual issues that reduce confidence: typos such as “continuos,” “dispite,” and “vers,” an apparent How2Sign duration error reported as “8080 hours,” duplicated/odd references, and a Figure 1 caption that appears to describe only the lipreading pipeline rather than the full MultiStream-LLM framework.

The limitations and societal-impact discussion are thin. For an accessibility-facing system, the paper should discuss failure modes across signers, dialects, lighting/occlusion, Deaf community evaluation, privacy implications of face/hand video, and risks of overclaiming translation reliability.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and under-addressed weakness of current sign language translation systems: fingerspelling, mouthings/non-manual cues, and their temporal asynchrony. The proposed decomposition into continuous signing, fingerspelling, lipreading, fusion, and LLM refinement is well motivated for real signed communication.

The reported empirical gains are large on How2Sign and BOBSL, and the paper includes useful ablations over components, LLM size, fusion strategy, temporal shifts, pretraining, and POS categories. The qualitative examples are also helpful for understanding how the pipeline behaves.

The supplementary material provides more implementation detail than the main paper, including pseudo-gloss prompts, architecture sizes, hyperparameters, computational cost, and failure modes such as proper-noun hallucination and semantic drift.
weaknesses: There are serious technical ambiguities in the core method. The dynamic routing module is described as routing segments, but the equations use temporal-average pooling to produce one sequence-level class for the whole clip. This seems incompatible with clips containing signing, fingerspelling, and rest periods, and undermines the claimed fine-grained expert selection.

The supervision design is not convincingly justified. Pseudo-glosses, phonemes, and fingerspelling labels are derived from English subtitles or rule-based detection rather than from aligned sign annotations. This makes it unclear whether the experts learn real sign-language structure or learn noisy proxies and dataset/language priors. The lipreading branch is especially questionable because generated English phonemes may not correspond to actual mouthings in the video.

The experimental evidence does not isolate the claimed contribution cleanly. The full system uses substantially larger visual encoders and a LLaMA-7B decoder, but comparisons to prior work do not control for model scale, pretrained components, LLM strength, or pseudo-label generation. The ablations show the LLM and lipreading dominate performance, but do not establish that the proposed routing/fusion design is necessary.

Several results and claims are internally inconsistent. In the supplementary fusion ablation, cross-attention obtains 22.3 BLEU-4 while gated fusion obtains 22.1, yet the text states gated fusion achieves comparable or superior performance. Table 4 mixes letter accuracy and BLEU-4 in a way that appears to span different tasks/datasets, making component effects hard to interpret.

Reproducibility is weak. Dataset splits, exact preprocessing, routing labels, pseudo-gloss generation protocol, GPT-4o version/settings, whether pseudo-labels will be released, and training details for BOBSL are insufficiently specified. The paper also reports very high computational requirements but lacks code or enough procedural detail to reproduce the pipeline.

The paper contains multiple citation and writing issues that reduce confidence: GPT-4o is cited as Radford and Narasimhan 2018, LipNet is cited incorrectly, several references are future or arXiv-style without clear provenance, and there are typos/inconsistent terminology throughout. These are not merely cosmetic because attribution and comparability are central to the claims.

The societal and linguistic validity aspects are underdeveloped. The method assumes English-derived pseudo-glosses and phonemes are adequate targets for ASL/BSL modeling, but this risks imposing spoken-language structure on signed languages. The BSL experiment is particularly under-explained given the linguistic differences from ASL.

strengths: The paper targets an important and under-addressed problem in sign language translation: integrating manual signing, fingerspelling, and mouth/lip cues rather than treating the video as a single undifferentiated stream.

The high-level modular idea is sensible. Specialized predictors for continuous signing, fingerspelling, and lipreading, followed by a fusion module and language-model refinement, is a plausible direction for improving robustness on names, technical terms, and non-manual cues.

The manuscript attempts to evaluate across multiple relevant settings, including How2Sign, BOBSL, and ChicagoFSWildPlus, and includes ablations for lipreading, fingerspelling, fusion, temporal shifts, and LLM size.
The qualitative examples are useful in showing the intended role of each stream and reveal some realistic failure modes such as proper-noun errors and semantic drift.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is not convincing enough to support the very strong claims of state-of-the-art performance. The comparisons mix systems with very different training data, model sizes, supervision, and pretraining regimes, but the paper does not provide a controlled comparison or sufficient protocol details to establish fairness.

There are serious internal inconsistencies in the reported results. For example, changing the LLM substantially changes reported letter accuracy, even though the LLM is described as mapping pseudo-glosses to English and should not directly affect fingerspelling letter accuracy. Similarly, fusion/temporal-alignment ablations report large changes in letter accuracy without clearly defining how this metric is computed in the full SLT pipeline.

The supervision pipeline is weakly justified. Pseudo-glosses are generated from English subtitles using GPT-4o, phoneme targets are derived from those pseudo-glosses, and potential fingerspelling is identified by rules over generated glosses. This creates noisy proxy labels, but the paper does not validate their quality, quantify error rates, or show that these labels correspond to what signers actually produce in the video.

The method description leaves important training details unresolved. The routing classifier is claimed to select sign/fingerspelling/rest segments, but the source of segment-level labels is not specified. The gating mechanism appears clip-level or feature-level rather than a demonstrated temporal alignment mechanism, despite the paper’s central claim about resolving asynchrony.

Several architectural claims are overstated relative to the actual formulation. Upsampling lip logits to the manual-stream length and applying a learned gate does not by itself establish asynchronicity-aware alignment. The temporal-shift ablation is also confusing, with inconsistent descriptions of shifts and no clear explanation of how learned alignment is implemented.

The paper has reproducibility problems. It lacks sufficient split details, preprocessing specifics, vocabulary construction, pseudo-gloss prompts, decoding settings for all comparisons, statistical variation, and clarity on whether external datasets overlap with evaluation content. Use of GPT-4o-generated annotations also raises reproducibility and accessibility concerns.

There are many presentation and consistency issues that undermine confidence: typos, equation errors, inconsistent total training time claims, inconsistent statements about full fine-tuning versus LoRA, and unclear table captions/metrics. These are not merely cosmetic because they affect interpretation of the scientific claims.

The claimed BOBSL generalization is particularly under-supported. The method uses ASL-oriented pseudo-gloss assumptions and then reports gains on BSL, but does not adequately address linguistic differences, subtitle alignment noise, or whether the pseudo-gloss generation procedure is appropriate for BSL.

The paper’s main empirical gains may be attributable to additional supervision, large external data, a much larger visual encoder, and a 7B LLM rather than to the proposed fusion mechanism. The ablations do not isolate these factors convincingly.

The limitations section acknowledges hallucination and semantic drift, but the evaluation relies heavily on BLEU/ROUGE and does not include human evaluation, signer/deaf-community validation, or targeted proper-noun/fingerspelling translation analysis despite those being central motivations.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and under-served problem in sign language translation: recovering information from fingerspelling and non-manual/lip cues that conventional single-stream SLT systems often miss. This is a meaningful computer vision contribution with clear practical motivation.

The proposed modular architecture is sensible and well matched to the problem: separate sign, fingerspelling, and lipreading experts, a routing/gating mechanism, temporal fusion, and an LLM decoder. The design directly targets asynchrony between manual and non-manual signals rather than treating it as incidental noise.

Experimental results are strong across multiple settings. The reported How2Sign BLEU-4 improvement from 15.5 to 22.1 is substantial, BOBSL improves over prior reported results, and ChicagoFSWildPlus letter accuracy improves over the strongest listed baseline. The gains are not limited to a single metric or dataset.

The ablation studies are useful and mostly support the architectural claims: removing lipreading, fusion, the sequencer, or the LLM substantially hurts performance; learned alignment outperforms fixed temporal shifts; and the comparison of fusion strategies helps justify the lightweight gated fusion choice.

The supplementary analysis is unusually informative. The POS breakdown, qualitative examples, pseudo-gloss details, parameter counts, training hyperparameters, and compute requirements improve clarity and make the model’s behavior easier to interpret.
The paper acknowledges important failure modes, especially proper noun hallucination and semantic drift under weak visual evidence, which is valuable for a high-impact accessibility application.
weaknesses: The evidence is strong but not fully airtight because comparisons may differ in training data, pretraining scale, model size, and use of external proprietary supervision. SignBind-LLM uses YouTube-ASL, ChicagoFSWildPlus, GPT-4o pseudo-glossing, DINOv2/ViT backbones, and LLaMA-2, while some baselines appear much smaller or trained under different regimes. The paper would be stronger with more controlled comparisons or compute/data-normalized baselines.

The reliance on GPT-4o-generated pseudo-glosses and phoneme targets raises reproducibility and attribution concerns. The exact prompts are given, but GPT-4o is proprietary and version-dependent; it is unclear whether the generated pseudo-label corpora will be released, and how sensitive the results are to pseudo-gloss quality.

Some methodological details remain ambiguous. The dynamic router is described as sequence-level, yet the system needs temporally localized switching between signing, fingerspelling, and rest. It is not fully clear how segment labels are obtained, how routing works for mixed sequences, or how errors from the router propagate through fusion.

The evaluation would benefit from more direct analysis of fingerspelled proper nouns inside full SLT, not only separate ChicagoFSWildPlus letter accuracy. Since one of the central claims is better preservation of names, places, and technical terms in translation, entity-level recall/precision on How2Sign or BOBSL would be highly relevant.

The LLM decoder may contribute substantial language-prior gains and hallucinations. The POS analysis itself shows overfitting to instructional-video discourse markers and weaker function-word behavior, while qualitative examples include semantically incorrect fluent outputs. More confidence calibration or faithfulness evaluation would strengthen the case for deployment-facing claims.

The paper contains some clarity and polish issues, including typos, inconsistent terminology, minor equation formatting problems, and a few over-broad claims such as being the first sign language LLM or establishing a new paradigm. These do not undermine the core contribution but should be tightened.
